findings.title: Outbound integration HTTP calls execute inside @Transactional methods, holding a Hikari DB connection across the remote round-trip
findings.category: Connection pool exhaustion / blocking I/O under transaction
findings.cvss: High — under a remote-system slowdown (ServiceNow/Splunk/CrowdStrike/Tenable degraded but not down), each in-flight push/poll pins one of only 20 (base) / 10 (dev) Hikari connections for the full remote latency. A burst of integration calls during a security incident (exactly when these adapters fire hardest) can drain the pool and stall ALL unrelated DB traffic platform-wide. Availability impact, not confidentiality/integrity.
findings.description: All four outbound integration services declare their public entry-point methods @Transactional and then invoke a synchronous, blocking remote HTTP client from inside that transaction. Spring opens (or borrows) a JDBC connection for the transaction at method entry and does not release it until the method returns. Because the remote HTTP call sits inside that boundary, the borrowed Hikari connection stays checked out for the ENTIRE network round-trip plus all in-thread retry sleeps. ServiceNowOutboundService.push() (line 83 @Transactional) calls client.createIncident() at line 109; SplunkOutboundService.push() (line 164 @Transactional) calls client.pushEvent() at line 176; CrowdStrikeOutboundService.containHost()/liftContainment()/hideHost() (lines 70/75/80 @Transactional) call client.* via runAction()->call.get() at line 111; TenableOutboundService.recastSeverity()/acceptRisk()/removeRecast() (lines 89/112/127 @Transactional) call client.* via runAction()->call.get() at line 162. The actual DB write (recordExternalLink / persistAuditRow / persistActionLog / persistRecastLog) is a sub-millisecond operation; the seconds-to-minutes are spent waiting on the remote socket while needlessly holding the connection.
findings.rootCause: The @Transactional boundary is drawn around the whole 'call remote system then persist outcome' unit of work instead of only around the persistence. There is no architectural separation between the I/O-bound remote call and the DB-bound audit write, so the connection is borrowed before the remote call begins and returned only after it completes.
findings.evidence: ServiceNowOutboundService.java:83-84 '@Transactional public ServiceNowIncidentResponse push(...)' then line 109 'ServiceNowIncidentResponse resp = client.createIncident(enriched);' (blocking) then line 110 'recordExternalLink(enriched, resp);' (the only DB work). Same shape in SplunkOutboundService.java:164 @Transactional / line 176 'resp = client.pushEvent(request);'. CrowdStrikeOutboundService.java:70 @Transactional / line 111 'resp = call.get();'. TenableOutboundService.java:89 @Transactional / line 162 'resp = call.get();'. Pool ceiling: application.yml:22 'maximum-pool-size: 20'; application-dev.yml:29 'maximum-pool-size: 10'.
findings.impact: With base maximum-pool-size=20, twenty concurrent slow integration pushes saturate the entire pool. Any unrelated request needing the DB then waits up to connection-timeout=30000ms (application.yml:24) and fails with a connection-timeout exception — a platform-wide stall triggered by a single sluggish third party. The integrations most likely to fire in bursts (CrowdStrike containment, Splunk SOC event push, ServiceNow incident creation) are exactly the ones invoked during an active security incident, so the failure mode peaks when the platform is needed most.
findings.reproduction: 1) Flip any adapter to LIVE (e.g. grc.integrations.servicenow.mode=LIVE) pointing at an endpoint that delays its response (e.g. a mock returning after 20s). 2) Fire 20 concurrent POST /api/v1/integrations/servicenow/test-push requests. 3) Observe all 20 Hikari connections checked out (GrcHikariPool active=20) for ~20s. 4) Concurrently issue any normal DB-backed request (e.g. GET /api/v1/risk/risks) — it blocks for up to 30s then throws a HikariPool connection-timeout. The leak-detection-threshold=60000 (application.yml:26) will also log 'Connection leak detection' warnings once a single retry chain exceeds 60s.
findings.resolution: Decouple the remote call from the transaction. Perform the blocking HTTP call OUTSIDE any @Transactional scope, then open a short, separate transaction only to persist the audit/external-link row. Concretely: remove @Transactional from the public push/poll methods; do the client.* call with no connection borrowed; then call a small @Transactional helper (e.g. an injected self-proxy method or a dedicated *PersistenceService.recordOutcome(...)) that writes the row and returns immediately. Better still, move the entire push off the request thread via @Async (the app already declares @EnableAsync on GrcApplication) or an outbox table drained by a worker, so request threads never block on third-party latency at all.

findings.title: Scheduled and manual integration polls hold one DB connection across the remote poll PLUS the entire per-finding ingest loop
findings.category: Long-lived transaction / connection hold across remote I/O + batch loop
findings.cvss: High — the @Transactional poll methods borrow a connection, make a multi-call blocking HTTP fetch (CrowdStrike does TWO sequential HTTP round-trips, with retries), then iterate the whole returned batch writing 3 rows per finding plus an audit row and a domain event, all inside the same transaction. One slow Tenable/Falcon endpoint or a large batch holds a scarce connection for the full duration and produces an oversized transaction that bloats the SQL Server Express log.
findings.description: TenableInboundService.pollFindings() (line 144 @Transactional) calls the blocking client.pollFindings() at line 158 BEFORE writing anything, then loops the returned batch calling ingestOne() (line 176) which performs three saves (vulnerabilities.save, findingLogRepo.save, linkRepo.save) plus audit.log and publisher.publishEvent per finding. The same shape is in CrowdStrikeInboundService.pollDetections() (line 142 @Transactional, blocking client.pollDetections() at line 156, ingestOne() per detection at line 172). CrowdStrike's poll is doubly expensive on I/O: LiveCrowdStrikeClient.pollDetections() (lines 79-115) makes TWO sequential remote calls — the ids query (line 82) then the bulk summaries fetch (line 98) — each wrapped in its own retry loop, all while the transaction's DB connection is held. The connection is checked out for: remote_latency + (retries x backoff) + N x (3 inserts + audit + event publish).
findings.rootCause: The remote fetch and the entire ingest batch share a single transactional/connection scope. The poll method opens the transaction, the connection is borrowed immediately, and it is not returned until the last finding in the batch is persisted — including the time spent on the remote HTTP fetch that does not need a DB connection at all.
findings.evidence: TenableInboundService.java:144 '@Transactional public int pollFindings()'; line 158 'batch = client.pollFindings();' (blocking, retries inside LiveTenableClient); lines 168-183 per-finding loop calling ingestOne() (lines 189-253: three .save() calls + audit.log + publishEvent). CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:142 '@Transactional public int pollDetections()'; line 156 'batch = client.pollDetections();'. LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:81-106 two sequential doWithRetryOn5xx() HTTP calls. Both polls are also driven by @Scheduled (TenableInboundService.java:119 fixedDelay 900s; CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:117 fixedDelay 60s) under @EnableScheduling (GrcApplication.java:24).
findings.impact: Each poll cycle consumes a pool connection for the full remote+ingest duration. With CrowdStrike polling every 60s and Tenable every 900s on a 10-connection dev pool (20 in base), a slow EDR/VM endpoint during heavy DB activity can tip the pool toward exhaustion. The long-running transaction also keeps locks and an open log section on SQL Server Express, contributing to the 10 GB Express size ceiling that the platform already monitors (application.yml:258-263 db-size health thresholds).
findings.reproduction: 1) Enable Tenable/CrowdStrike LIVE + pollingEnabled=true against a mock returning a 500-finding batch after a 10s delay. 2) Watch GrcHikariPool active-connection metric (actuator /metrics) jump by one and stay elevated for remote_delay + ingest_time. 3) Manually trigger pollFindings() via the controller concurrently with the scheduled loop and N concurrent app requests; observe connection-acquisition latency on unrelated endpoints climb. 4) Inspect the SQL Server transaction log growth during a large ingest — a single transaction spans the whole batch.
findings.resolution: Fetch the remote batch with NO transaction open (move client.poll*() out of the @Transactional method), then persist findings in short, per-finding (or small-chunk) transactions so each borrows and returns a connection quickly. This caps connection-hold time at a single DB write, lets other work interleave, and keeps SQL Server transactions small. Pattern: pollOnce() (no @Transactional) -> List<Dto> = client.poll(); for (dto : batch) persistence.ingestOne(orgId, dto) where ingestOne is @Transactional(propagation=REQUIRES_NEW) on a separate bean.

findings.title: In-thread Thread.sleep retry/backoff inside transactional integration calls extends DB-connection hold time to as much as ~75s-2min
findings.cvss: Medium — the retry loops in the LIVE clients block the calling (request or scheduler) thread with Thread.sleep between attempts. Because the call originates inside an open transaction (PERF-IO-001/002), the backoff sleeps are added on top of the remote latency to the connection-hold time, multiplying the pool-exhaustion window. Bounded but large worst case; depends on a failing remote system.
findings.description: Every LIVE client retries 5xx/connection failures with an in-thread exponential backoff that calls Thread.sleep on the calling thread. Splunk and CrowdStrike cap the per-attempt backoff at BACKOFF_CAP_MS = 30_000L (LiveSplunkClient.java:49, LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:54) over up to 3 attempts. ServiceNow's withRetry (LiveServiceNowClient.java:194-216) sleeps starting at 250ms, doubling, capped at 5000ms, with max-retries=3 (so up to 4 attempts) and a read timeout of 30s per attempt (ServiceNowProperties timeout-seconds=30, application.yml:183). Because these clients are called from inside @Transactional service methods, the entire sleep+timeout budget is added to the DB-connection-hold time. ServiceNow worst case approaches 4 x 30s read timeout + backoffs ~= 2 minutes; Splunk/CrowdStrike approach 3 x 5s timeout + ~30s+ backoff ~= 45-75s.
findings.rootCause: Retry/backoff is implemented synchronously on the calling thread (Thread.sleep) AND the call is made while a transaction (and therefore a pooled connection) is open. The two together convert transient remote failures into prolonged connection occupancy.
findings.evidence: LiveSplunkClient.java:99 'sleep(delayMs);' line 100 'delayMs = (long) Math.min(BACKOFF_CAP_MS, ...)' with BACKOFF_CAP_MS=30_000 (line 49) and maxAttempts from props (default retry max-attempts=3). LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:192 'sleep(delayMs);' line 193 cap 30_000 (line 54). LiveServiceNowClient.java:207 'Thread.sleep(backoffMs);' line 212 'backoffMs = Math.min(backoffMs * 2, 5000);' with attempts = maxRetries+1 (line 195) and read timeout 30s (ServiceNowIntegrationConfig.java:61 setReadTimeout(props.getTimeoutSeconds())). All invoked from @Transactional service methods (see PERF-IO-001).
findings.impact: A degraded third party (intermittent 503s, slow responses) turns each push into a connection held for tens of seconds to ~2 minutes. With only 20 (base) / 10 (dev) connections, even a handful of concurrent retrying pushes meaningfully shrinks the pool's effective capacity, and the leak-detection-threshold of 60s (application.yml:26) will start emitting false 'connection leak' warnings on the longest ServiceNow retry chains — masking real leaks in operational logs.
findings.reproduction: 1) Point ServiceNow LIVE at an endpoint returning HTTP 503 on every attempt. 2) Call POST /test-push. 3) Observe the request thread (and its borrowed connection) blocked for ~ (4 x 30s) + (0.25+0.5+1.0s) ~= 121s before failing. 4) Repeat 20x concurrently and watch GrcHikariPool exhaust and unrelated DB calls time out at 30s.
findings.resolution: First and primarily, remove the remote call from the transaction (PERF-IO-001) so retry sleeps no longer occupy a connection. Additionally, prefer non-blocking retry (Resilience4j / Spring Retry with a separate scheduler, or async + outbox) over Thread.sleep, and lower the ServiceNow read timeout from 30s toward the 5s the other adapters use unless a specific SLA requires longer. Cap total retry budget (sum of timeouts + backoffs) well under the 60s leak-detection threshold and the 30s connection-timeout to avoid cascading symptoms.

findings.title: OAuth token refresh performs a synchronized blocking HTTP fetch while a transaction holds a DB connection, serialising all callers
findings.category: Synchronized blocking I/O on hot path inside transaction
findings.cvss: Medium — token refresh (every ~1h, or on any 401) runs a blocking HTTP POST under a single object monitor (synchronized) and is reached from inside the @Transactional push path via the auth-header callback. During refresh, one thread blocks on the remote token endpoint while holding both its DB connection and the lock; every other caller needing a token blocks on that lock, so a slow token endpoint stalls multiple integration requests at once.
findings.description: ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.getAccessToken() (line 53) and refresh() (line 61) are both 'synchronized' on the manager instance. refresh() performs a blocking restClient.post() to the token URL (lines 76-81). getAccessToken() is invoked from LiveServiceNowClient.authHeader() (lines 137-147), which runs while building every outbound request — i.e. inside the @Transactional push()/update() flow. When the cached token is within the 60s expiry skew (line 33 EXPIRY_SKEW) or after a 401, the next caller triggers a blocking remote fetch while holding the monitor; all other threads calling getAccessToken() queue behind that lock. Combined with PERF-IO-001, the refreshing thread also holds its pooled DB connection for the duration of the token fetch.
findings.rootCause: A coarse-grained 'synchronized' guards the entire refresh including the blocking network call, rather than only the cached-slot read/write, so the remote latency is held under the lock. The refresh is reached transitively from within an open transaction, compounding the connection-hold problem.
findings.evidence: ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.java:53 'public synchronized String getAccessToken()'; line 61 'public synchronized String refresh()'; lines 76-81 blocking 'restClient.post()....body(Map.class)' inside the synchronized method. Reached via LiveServiceNowClient.java:139-140 'case OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS -> h.setBearerAuth(tokenManager.getAccessToken());' inside authHeader(), called from createIncident()/getIncident()/updateIncident() which run under ServiceNowOutboundService @Transactional methods. CrowdStrike has the analogous CrowdStrikeOAuthTokenManager used by LiveCrowdStrikeClient.authHeader() (LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:234-239).
findings.impact: On token expiry (hourly) or a Falcon/ServiceNow secret rotation (401 path), the first integration push pays the full token-endpoint latency under the lock and under an open transaction; concurrent integration requests block on the lock and cannot proceed, amplifying connection-hold and tail latency precisely during credential refresh windows. A slow or flaky token endpoint can briefly serialise the whole integration subsystem.
findings.reproduction: 1) ServiceNow LIVE with OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS; point token-url at an endpoint that delays the token response by 10s. 2) Let the cached token reach the 60s expiry skew. 3) Fire several concurrent /test-push calls. 4) Observe exactly one thread doing the token fetch (10s) while the others block on the monitor, all within their transactions/connections; measure the resulting 10s tail on every concurrent push.
findings.resolution: Narrow the lock so the blocking HTTP fetch happens outside the monitor (double-checked refresh, or single-flight via AtomicReference + a separate guarded fetch), and ensure token acquisition does not occur inside an open DB transaction (fixed transitively by PERF-IO-001 moving the whole client call out of @Transactional). Optionally refresh tokens proactively on a background scheduler before expiry so the request path never pays refresh latency.

findings.title: Hikari pool sizing (base=20 / dev=10) is undersized for blocking-integration workloads and dev overrides drop leak-detection visibility
findings.cvss: Low — sizing itself is reasonable for pure DB work against SQL Server Express, but given the blocking-I/O-under-transaction patterns (PERF-IO-001..004) the effective pool capacity is much lower than the nominal 20/10. The k6 breakpoint run did not reach an error threshold in the captured log (no failed iterations through ~67 VUs / ~325 iters/s on a read-only endpoint that does not touch the integration paths), so this is a forward-looking sizing/observability concern rather than an observed outage.
findings.description: The base Hikari pool is maximum-pool-size=20 with minimum-idle=5, connection-timeout=30000, leak-detection-threshold=60000 (application.yml:21-26). The dev profile overrides ONLY minimum-idle (2) and maximum-pool-size (10) (application-dev.yml:27-29), inheriting the base connection-timeout and leak-detection-threshold. Two observations: (1) Sizing of 20 is fine for CPU-bound DB work on SQL Server Express (Express has no hard low connection cap; the real Express limits are ~1.4 GB buffer pool / 4 cores / 10 GB data), but it is small once connections are routinely tied up for seconds-to-minutes by the blocking integration paths — the formula connections = ((core_count x 2) + effective_spindle_count) assumes connections are released quickly, which the integration code violates. (2) The leak-detection-threshold=60000 is below the worst-case integration connection-hold computed in PERF-IO-003 (~121s for ServiceNow), so once those slow paths run they will emit spurious leak warnings, eroding trust in the leak detector. The k6 load.js exercises only GET /api/v1/risk/risks (load.js readRisks), which never touches the integration adapters, so the load test does not characterise the at-risk path.
findings.rootCause: Pool size and connection-timeout were tuned for fast DB-only requests; the integration adapters' blocking-under-transaction behaviour was not accounted for, so nominal pool capacity overstates real capacity. The leak-detection threshold is not aligned with the (unintended) long connection holds the integration code can produce.
findings.evidence: application.yml:22 'maximum-pool-size: 20'; :24 'connection-timeout: 30000'; :26 'leak-detection-threshold: 60000'. application-dev.yml:29 'maximum-pool-size: 10' (overrides only size + minimum-idle; inherits the rest). k6 load.js: readRisks() hits GET /api/v1/risk/risks only; k6.log shows the breakpoint scenario climbing to ~67 VUs / ~325.75 iters/s with '0 interrupted iterations' and no captured error spike (the log ends mid-breakpoint at ~93%; no final handleSummary block / k6-summary.json was produced).
findings.impact: Under any real integration load the platform behaves as if it had far fewer than 20 connections, making pool exhaustion (PERF-IO-001/002) reachable at modest concurrency. The mismatch between leak-detection-threshold (60s) and integration connection-hold (up to ~121s) will generate misleading leak warnings. The current load test gives false confidence because it does not exercise the integration code paths.
findings.reproduction: 1) Compare application.yml:19-26 vs application-dev.yml:27-29 — confirm dev inherits connection-timeout/leak-detection from base. 2) Note k6 load.js exercises only a read endpoint. 3) Combine with the PERF-IO-001 reproduction to show exhaustion at < 20 concurrent integration pushes despite a nominal pool of 20.
findings.resolution: Primary fix is PERF-IO-001..004 (stop holding connections across remote I/O). Independently: (a) make the integration HTTP work run on a bounded, separate executor/outbox so it cannot consume the primary DB pool at all; (b) once remote calls are out of transactions, keep maximum-pool-size=20 for base but add a dedicated, smaller bounded thread pool for outbound integration work; (c) raise leak-detection-threshold above the realistic worst-case hold OR (preferably) reduce the worst-case hold below 60s so the existing threshold stays meaningful; (d) extend the k6 suite with a scenario that drives the integration endpoints (test-push / poll) to characterise the actually-at-risk path.
findings.patchBefore:
# application.yml
hikari:
  maximum-pool-size: 20
  connection-timeout: 30000
  leak-detection-threshold: 60000
# application-dev.yml (overrides only size + idle)
hikari:
  minimum-idle: 2
  maximum-pool-size: 10
findings.patchAfter:
# Keep DB pool for fast DB work; run integration HTTP off-pool (async/outbox).
# After PERF-IO-001..004, integration calls no longer borrow DB connections, so
# 20 (base) / 10 (dev) is adequate. Ensure leak-detection-threshold stays above the
# realistic max DB-only transaction time (now << 60s) so it flags only true leaks.
# Add a k6 scenario that exercises /api/v1/integrations/*/test-push to load-test the
# real at-risk path (current load.js hits only GET /api/v1/risk/risks).
